parts: Section 212, row K. I've been to every home game since freshman year and I have never heard the student section go that quiet. Down by three, under two minutes left, and the kid two seats over from me, the one in gold body paint who had been screaming since warmups, just sat down and put his face in his hands.

Then the interception. I don't remember standing up. I remember gold paint all over my sleeve because he grabbed me and would not let go, and a woman a row behind us crying into a hot dog wrapper like it was a handkerchief. Nobody around us knew each other. For about four minutes it didn't matter.
characters: the kid in gold body paint
the woman crying into a hot dog wrapper

parts: Yes, I was the kid in the gold paint. It took forty minutes to put on and my roommate did my back with the sponge from our kitchen sink, which I am only now realizing was a mistake.

I didn't give up when we went down three. I sat down because my legs were shaking. When the pick happened I grabbed the first human I could reach, a guy in a gray hoodie who smelled like sunscreen, and I'm sorry about your sleeve. I'm not sorry about the hug.
characters: the guy in the gray hoodie I grabbed

parts: My son is a freshman and I drove up from Naples for his first home game. He spent the night with his friends, which is exactly right, and texted me 'look at the 30 yard line' and I could not find him in all that noise.

When they intercepted it, I cried. Into a hot dog wrapper, apparently, which a stranger has now written down for the internet. Fine. I'd do it again. I found him after, hoarse and grinning, and he let me hug him in front of his friends.
characters: my son, somewhere in the student section

parts: My mom drove four hours to watch a game she does not understand, and I spent the first half pretending she wasn't texting me every eight minutes.

We were down by the 30 when the tuba player turned around and winked at our whole row, like he knew. Two plays later, the pick. I looked for my mom in the stands and obviously couldn't see her, so I just waved at all of them.
characters: the tuba player who winked at our row

parts: For the record, I wink at the student section every game. It has never once worked before. Our director says the fight song does not cause interceptions. Our director was not in the stands on October 3rd.

Lot 7, same spot for eleven seasons. Burgers on at noon, kickoff at seven, and somewhere in between a couple in a dented silver Civic two rows over could not get it to turn over. I had cables. I always have cables.

Their battery was older than the kid in the passenger seat. While we waited for it to take a charge, a grown man in a full suit of plastic knight armor walked up, said nothing, and ate three of my burgers standing in the sun. I never caught his name. He saluted when he left.
characters: the couple with the dead Civic
the guy in the full knight costume

parts: Our car died in Lot 7 forty minutes before kickoff, which is a sentence I would like to never type again. Dan wanted to call a tow truck. I wanted to cry. A man at a grill two rows over had jumper cables out before either of us finished.

We missed the first quarter and I do not care. We made it to our seats in time to see the interception, and I spent the drive home trying to figure out how you thank a stranger who fixed your night and also fed you.
characters: the man at the grill with the jumper cables

parts: The armor is vacuum-formed plastic and it is ninety degrees in October. By the time I reached Lot 7 I was mostly sweat and regret. A man with a grill handed me a burger without a word, and then another one, and then I stopped counting.

I wore the helmet the whole game. Section 104, row C. When the pick happened I raised my sword and a little kid behind me raised a churro, and I think that is the most knightly thing I have ever done.
characters: the grill guy who fed me three burgers

parts: Concession stand 14, nachos and pretzels. We sold out of cheese at halftime, which has happened twice in my life. The line went back past the restrooms.

Right before the fourth quarter a dad came up holding a mason jar of quarters with his little girl on his shoulders. She had saved them all summer. I counted every one with forty people behind them and nobody complained. Twenty-two dollars exactly.
characters: the dad holding a jar of quarters

parts: My daughter saved quarters from May to October for 'stadium nachos', which she had seen on TV and decided were the point of football. I was sure we would hold up the line and get yelled at.

The guy at stand 14 counted every quarter out loud with her, slowly, like it was the most important transaction of his night. She ate the nachos during the interception and missed it entirely. She says it was the best game she has ever been to.
characters: the nacho guy at stand 14

parts: I work section 230. My job is to face the crowd, so I have never really seen a game. I see the games on people's faces instead.

Down by three with two minutes left, my whole section looked like a waiting room. Then I heard the roar from the other side of the stadium half a second before my section understood, and I watched four hundred faces change at once. That is my favorite part of the job, and nobody ever asks about it.

Top row, binoculars, because I like to watch the whole stadium instead of the ball. In the third quarter someone on the far side kept flashing a phone light in a pattern, three short and one long, every few minutes.
Right after the interception it stopped and never started again. I asked around on the way out. Nobody else had seen it. If that was you, I would really like to know what it meant.
characters: whoever was flashing the phone light

posts.body: Still finding gold paint in my ears. Worth it.
I read all five of these out loud to my husband. He says he is coming to the next one.
Same seats for the next home game. Gray hoodie optional, gold paint encouraged.
Band vote is in: the wink stays.
Rob, I owe you a battery and at least one burger.
Lot 7, same spot, next home game. Bring the knight.
The knight will be there. The knight is bringing his own burgers this time.
She wants to know if you take nickels.

parts: We open at seven. By eight the water was over the curb and a man in a full suit came in barefoot, holding his shoes in one hand and his laptop over his head with the other. He ordered a cortado like nothing was happening.

A girl with a nursing school backpack asked if we had a mop, and then just stayed and used it for an hour. An older guy at the window kept telling everyone this was nothing, 1992 was worse. Nobody left until the street drained.
characters: the man in the suit holding his shoes
the girl who stayed to help mop
the old man who said 1992 was worse

parts: I had a 9 a.m. pitch on Brickell and a car that is not a boat. I walked the last two blocks with my shoes in my hand. The barista with a pencil behind her ear gave me a towel for my feet and wouldn't let me pay for the cortado.
I did the pitch from the corner table over the cafe wifi. We got the meeting moved, not won, but I'll take moved. I owe that place a lot of cortados.
characters: the barista with a pencil behind her ear

parts: My clinical got cancelled because of the rain and I was not going to sit in my apartment. I asked for a mop mostly as a joke. Then it was handed to me.
There's something about pushing water out of a door with strangers that makes it feel like a party. The man by the window narrated the entire thing like a sports commentator.
characters: the man by the window narrating everything

parts: I said it and I'll say it again: 1992 was worse. I was a young man in Homestead when Andrew came through. A wet floor and a closed street is a Thursday.
But I'll admit the kids handled it well. The girl with the mop, the boy in the suit with no shoes. Good kids. I bought the next round of pastelitos.

parts: Got off a twelve at eleven and I was out of scrubs. Dryer six has been eating quarters since the summer and someone had taped a sign to it that just said KICK HERE, with an arrow.

A guy was asleep on the folding table with his head on a Seminoles blanket. A woman I'd never seen was folding a load that clearly wasn't hers, very neatly. I kicked where the arrow said. It started. I still don't know who made that sign.
characters: the guy asleep on the folding table
the woman folding someone else's laundry
whoever taped the KICK HERE sign

parts: I put my clothes in, sat on the table to wait, and woke up forty minutes later with all of it folded into perfect squares. The nurse in navy scrubs told me a stranger did it and left. I have never been so cared for by someone I didn't meet.
characters: the nurse in navy scrubs

parts: I will not apologize. His load had been sitting in that dryer for forty minutes, it was going to wrinkle, and he was clearly asleep for a reason. Folding is calming. I fold at my sister's house too and she also finds it strange.

It was me. I made the sign in July. Dryer six has a loose panel on the left side, and a firm kick just below the coin slot reseats it. I've told the owner. Until it's fixed, the sign stays, and I'm glad it worked for someone at midnight.

parts: Our team is called Dewey Decimal Destroyers and we have lost every Wednesday since March. Round five was ancient history and the table next to us answered Mesopotamia to every single question.
They were right four times. We came in second by one point. I have never respected and resented a group of strangers more.
characters: the team that answered Mesopotamia to everything

parts: It was a strategy. If you don't know, say Mesopotamia. The cradle of civilization covers a lot of ground. The Dewey Decimal team kept glaring at us, which only made it more fun.
I write the questions on Tuesdays. Round five was supposed to be the hard one. One table guessed the same word nine times and won the night. I'm rewriting round five.

arcs.place: Edward Ball Wakulla Springs State Park
arcs.title: Manatees under the dive tower

parts: Cold front came through and the water was so clear you could count the eelgrass. Three manatees were parked under the dive tower like they owned it. A little girl in a pink life jacket narrated their names to everyone on the dock: Biscuit, Tuesday and Mr. Big.
characters: the girl in the pink life jacket naming the manatees

parts: I work the boat tours. Every cold snap the manatees come into the spring, and every cold snap a child names them. This year it was Biscuit, Tuesday and Mr. Big. Honestly, better than last year's names.

Six a.m. birding is supposed to be peaceful. I came around the bend on the boardwalk and there was a six foot alligator lying across it, completely still, like a speed bump with teeth. I waited eleven minutes. It did not move. I went the long way and saw a purple gallinule, so I'm calling it even.

There's a gator who likes the sunny stretch of boardwalk near the first overlook. Regulars just wait or turn around. I watched a student in a Gators cap stand there forever before going the long way. Smart kid.

The show let out at one and half the crowd ended up at Bills. I sat at the counter next to a girl who was still wearing a paper wristband and humming the encore. We split a short stack and argued about whether the second song was a cover.
It was. I looked it up. I didn't get her number, but I'd know that wristband anywhere.
characters: the girl humming the encore at the counter

parts: I was humming. I hum when I'm happy and also when I'm wrong about covers, apparently. If the guy who split the short stack with me reads this: you were right, and the syrup was yours.
characters: the guy who split the short stack

parts: Concert nights are my favorite and my worst. Fifty pancakes in an hour. Two kids at the counter shared a short stack and talked about music the whole time like they'd known each other for years.

arcs.title: Giant bubbles on the big lawn

parts: Every other Saturday I bring a bucket of dish soap, glycerin and a secret amount of cornstarch to the big lawn by the river, plus two sticks and a loop of cotton rope. On a still afternoon one bubble can get as long as a car. This Saturday the wind dropped around four and I knew it was going to be a good one.

A little one in dinosaur rain boots chased every single bubble with her dad running two steps behind, apologizing to everyone she bumped into. And a man got off a rental bike on the Riverwalk, leaned it on a tree, sat down in the grass and did not move for an hour. When I packed up he helped me carry the bucket to my car.
characters: the dad chasing a toddler in dinosaur rain boots
the man who parked his rental bike and stayed

parts: My daughter wore her dinosaur rain boots because it said thirty percent chance of rain, and also because she wears them to everything, including the pool. We came for the playground. We never made it to the playground. A man was making bubbles the size of a minivan and she decided that her job, her only job, was to pop all of them.

I said sorry to roughly forty strangers in one hour. Nobody minded. A woman on a picnic blanket was drawing the bubbles and she turned her clipboard around to show my daughter, who announced that the drawing was wrong because it did not have her in it. The woman added a tiny dinosaur boot in the corner.
characters: the woman drawing on a picnic blanket

parts: I moved to Tampa in August for a job and I still do not know anyone outside my office. Saturdays have been long. I rented a bike to ride the whole Riverwalk because a coworker said it was the thing to do, and halfway along I saw a bubble float over the railing, bigger than any bubble has a right to be.

I sat down to watch for a minute and stayed until the sun went orange. A woman a few feet away was sketching on a clipboard and asked if she could put me in the drawing, since I had not moved in so long. I said yes. The man with the bubbles let me try the sticks once. I made a bad one. Everyone clapped anyway.
characters: the woman sketching on a clipboard

parts: I draw at Curtis Hixon most weekends because the light comes off the river sideways in the late afternoon and makes everything look like it is lit from inside. Giant bubbles are the hardest thing I have ever tried to draw. They are every color and no color, and they never hold still long enough.

So I drew the people instead. A man who had been sitting so still he could have been a statue, his rental bike leaned against a tree. A toddler in dinosaur rain boots who critiqued my work and was right. Her dad, mid-apology. By sunset I had one full page, and it is the best page in the book.
characters: the toddler's dad, mid-apology

parts: First time on a paddleboard, and I made it from the boat launch to the edge of the park before I turned to wave at my sister and my sunglasses slid right off my head into the river. They were prescription. I said a word I will not repeat on a family website.

A teenager fishing off the seawall saw the whole thing. He swung his crabbing net down on its long pole, scooped twice, and came up with my glasses and one very confused crab. He handed them down to me like it was nothing. I said thank you in English, then in Spanish, then somehow in French, which I do not speak.
characters: the teenager on the seawall with a crabbing net

parts: I crab off the seawall by the park most Saturdays with chicken necks and a string. My grandpa taught me on this same wall. You learn to watch the water, not your phone, and that is how I saw the paddleboarder's sunglasses go in. They sank slow, right by the pilings.

Two scoops and I had them. Also a blue crab, who I put back. She said thank you in about three languages, one of which I am pretty sure she invented. I am nineteen and nobody has ever thanked me that hard for anything. I went home and told my grandpa and he laughed until he coughed.
characters: the paddleboarder who said thank you in three languages

parts: When I got to the lawn around two there was a green folding chair set up facing the river, perfectly level, with a paperback face down on the seat and a thermos tucked in the cup holder. Nobody near it. I figured whoever owned it had gone for a bathroom or a snack and would be back in five minutes.

At six it was still there. The book was a mystery, fittingly, open to page two hundred and twelve. I did not touch anything. When I left after sunset the chair was gone, and I never saw anyone pick it up. If it was yours, I hope you liked the ending.
characters: whoever left the green folding chair

posts.body: I scanned the page. Gil, Ro, I can send you both a copy. The dinosaur boot stays in the corner.
Two weeks from Saturday, same lawn? I will bring the bike back and actually try to make a good one.
She has asked about the bubble man every day since. Please confirm you exist so I can stop being questioned.
I exist. Wind permitting, the bucket will be there.
I would like the record to show I have since bought a strap for my glasses.
The crab would like the record to show it was having a normal day before this.

parts: The beach at Fort Zach is rocky and everybody warns you about it, and everybody is right, and it is still the best snorkeling you can walk into from the sand. I spent the late afternoon floating over the rocks while a college kid next to me in a mask two sizes too big narrated every fish to nobody.

When the light went gold we all climbed out and sat on the rocks to wait for the sun. An older man near me had a little notebook and wrote something down the second it touched the water. I asked. He said he has been counting sunsets for years. This was one of the good ones, he said, and underlined it.
characters: the college kid in the oversized snorkel mask
the man counting sunsets in a notebook

parts: I borrowed my roommate's snorkel mask, and my roommate has a much larger head than me, which I learned about four seconds into the water. I spent the whole swim holding it on with one hand and yelling into the snorkel every time I saw something. Parrotfish. Another parrotfish. A thing that was maybe a rock.

The woman floating next to me finally lifted her head and said 'that one is a sergeant major,' and I said 'thank you' through the snorkel, which came out as a long honk. Later on the rocks a couple a little way down started clapping for the sunset, and I clapped too, because I had never seen anything like it.
characters: the snorkeler who told me the fish names
the couple who clapped for the sunset

parts: My wife and I started writing down sunsets in 2009, one line each, place and color. She kept the book and I kept the pen. Since she passed I keep both. I go to Fort Zach on Sundays because she liked how the sun drops right between the ships and the shore.

That evening a young woman with salt in her hair asked what I was writing, and I told her, which I do not usually do. Then a couple down the rocks clapped when the sun went under, the way people used to on Mallory Square. I wrote it down: orange, then pink, applause. That is a good line. She would have liked it.
characters: the young woman who asked about my notebook

parts: We got married on Thursday in a courthouse in Ohio and flew to Key West on Friday with one carry-on each. We had a list. Sunday's item was 'sunset somewhere that isn't Mallory Square,' because we wanted it to be quiet. We found the rocks at Fort Zach and a kid in a huge snorkel mask honking at fish.

When the sun touched the water I clapped. I don't know why. My husband laughed and joined in, and then the kid in the mask clapped too, and an older man with a notebook looked up and smiled at us like he knew something. I keep thinking about that smile. I think it was a blessing.
characters: the kid in the huge snorkel mask
the older man with a notebook

parts: I took my ring off to put on sunscreen, set it on my towel, and somehow when I shook the towel out the ring went with the sand into the shallows. It was my grandmother's. I was on my knees in six inches of water with my phone flashlight, nearly crying, while the sun went down behind me.

A guy in a mask and fins was just coming in. He asked what I'd lost, said 'give me two minutes,' and went face down in the water like a heron. It took him more like twenty minutes. He came up holding the ring between two fingers and said 'this one?' as if there could be another.
characters: the snorkeler who came up holding my ring

parts: I snorkel Fort Zach after work most days when the water is clear, and I've found a lot of things on the bottom there: sunglasses, a fork, once a whole flip-flop with a fish living in it. I was walking out when I saw a woman on her knees at the edge of the water, holding her phone light over the sand.

A ring in the shallows is easier than it sounds if you keep your shadow off it. The light was going so I stayed low and slow. When I found it she did not say anything for a second, just held it with both hands. Then she hugged me, fins and all. Best thing I've ever pulled off that bottom.
characters: the woman searching the shallows by phone light

posts.body: We read this on the plane home and both cried in row 23. Thank you for writing down our clap.
It is in the book now. Orange, then pink, applause. All four of you are in that line.
Update: bought my own mask. It fits. I miss the honk a little.
Showed my grandmother's ring to my mom and told her the whole story. She wants to buy you dinner.
Tell her I accept. Also tell her to keep that towel away from the water.

arcs.title: The morning the swell came in

parts: Swell forecast said chest high and clean for Saturday morning and for once the forecast told the truth. I was in the water at Hanna by six-forty, sets rolling in long and glassy, the kind of morning you tell people about for a year. Every surfer in Duval County had the same idea by seven.

Between sets I watched a first-timer on a blue foam board try to stand up maybe thirty times, so I started yelling 'paddle, paddle, now stand' when her wave came. On the beach an old man was doing tai chi right at the waterline, slow as anything, while a dog ran circles around him carrying something in its mouth.
characters: the first-timer on the blue foam board
the old man doing tai chi at the waterline

parts: I turned forty this year and my list said 'learn to surf,' so I bought the biggest, bluest foam board at the store and drove to Hanna Park at dawn like a person with a plan. I did not have a plan. I had a board and a lot of confidence and no idea which way the waves were going.

Thirty-one falls. I counted. On thirty-two a guy out past me started yelling 'paddle, paddle, now stand,' and I did all three in that order, and I rode it maybe four seconds all the way to where the water was shin deep. I screamed. He screamed. A woman on the beach chasing her dog screamed too, I think just to be included.
characters: the surfer yelling 'paddle, paddle, now stand'

parts: I am seventy-six and I do my form at the edge of the water every morning I can get to Hanna. The sand is soft, which keeps the knees honest. That Saturday was crowded with surfers, the water full of black wetsuits like seals, and I liked the company.

Halfway through, a sandy brown dog sat down in front of me and dropped a crab shell at my feet like a gift. Then it watched me, very seriously, through the whole second half of the form. Its owner arrived out of breath and apologized. I told her it had better posture than most of my class.
characters: the woman whose dog brought me a crab shell

parts: Biscuit is a two-year-old mutt with exactly one hobby: finding things on the beach and giving them to strangers. I unclipped her for one second at the dog-friendly end to fix my shoe and she was gone down the sand at full speed toward a man doing tai chi.

By the time I caught up she had given him a crab shell and was sitting perfectly, like a dog in a commercial. He told me she had better posture than his students. Then a woman out in the water stood up on a blue board and rode all the way in, and I screamed with her, because what else do you do.
characters: the woman who rode the blue board all the way in

parts: While everyone was on the beach I walked the bike trails around the lake. Every quarter mile or so there was a small rock at the base of a tree, painted bright, each with one or two words in white letters. The first one said 'keep.' The next one said 'going.' Then 'you're.' Then 'almost.'

I followed them for two miles. The last rock I found, back near the lake, said 'there,' and nothing came after it. I sat on the bench by the water for a while anyway. I don't know who painted them or what they meant for, but that Saturday they were for me.
characters: whoever painted the rocks on the lake trail

posts.body: Went back Sunday. Stood up on the ninth try. Nobody yelled and I missed it.
Next swell, I will be out there yelling. Paddle, paddle, now stand.
Biscuit is welcome in my class any morning. She can bring a shell.

parts: There is a free sunrise yoga class on the grass at Vinoy Park on Sunday mornings, and I finally went, and I forgot my mat. I stood at the back holding my car keys and a coffee while forty people unrolled theirs in perfect rows facing the water.

A man next to me looked at my empty hands, pulled a beach towel out of his bag, gave it to me and did the whole class on the bare grass. He said he wanted the grass anyway. I do not believe him. When we lay down at the end, the sky over the bay went pink and a pelican landed close enough to hear.
characters: the man who gave me his beach towel

parts: I always bring a beach towel in case the grass is wet, and the grass is always wet. On Sunday a woman showed up next to me with a coffee and no mat, looking like she was about to leave, so I handed her the towel. I said I liked the grass. The grass was very wet.

In front of us a woman laughed through every single balance pose, not a little laugh, a full laugh, which made her fall over, which made her laugh harder. By tree pose half the back row was wobbling and giggling with her. I have been to that class for a year and it was the best one.
characters: the woman who laughed through every balance pose

parts: I cannot balance. My doctor says it is my inner ear. My sister says it is my personality. Either way, at sunrise yoga I fall over during tree pose, and when I fall over I laugh, and I cannot stop once I start.

Sunday I started early, during warrior three, and by tree pose the whole back row was going. A man behind me on bare wet grass was laughing so hard he had to lie down. The instructor just smiled and said 'balance is a practice.' I'm going back next week. The back row needs me.
characters: the man laughing on the wet grass behind me

parts: My husband walked our dog along the Vinoy waterfront every morning for eleven years. Since spring it has been me, and for months I took a different route because I could not do the park. On Sunday the dog pulled me that way and I let him.

There was a yoga class on the grass, forty people lying still under a pink sky, and the dog stopped and sat down to watch them like he was waiting his turn. Nobody noticed us. We stayed until they all sat up. I think I will come back next Sunday. I think he knew the way better than I did.

posts.body: Washed the towel. Bringing it back Sunday, and I bought a mat. And a second towel, for whoever forgets next.
Back row, Sunday, seven sharp. Bring your worst tree pose.

parts: I throw a cast net off the seawall at Bayfront for bait most evenings. You stand still long enough and the bay tells you things. That Saturday it told me dolphins, two of them, working the bait schools right along the wall, close enough to hear them breathe.

Two young people on a bench were so busy being nervous with each other they hadn't seen them, so I pointed. They both jumped up and leaned on the rail. Down the wall, a woman with a camera lens as long as my arm swung it around in time. I went home with no bait and a good evening.
characters: the two people on what was obviously a first date
the woman with the long camera lens

parts: We had been talking on an app for three weeks and agreed on a walk at Bayfront at sunset because a walk is easy to leave. Neither of us left. We sat on a bench and talked about nothing, and I could not tell you one word of it now, and I don't care.

An older man with a fishing net turned around and said 'you two are missing it,' and pointed, and there were dolphins right below the rail. She grabbed my arm. That is the part I remember. Later, a woman with a big camera showed us a photo she had taken of the dolphins, and we were in the corner of it, leaning on the rail.
characters: the man with the cast net who told us to look

parts: I photograph birds at Bayfront in the evenings. Pelicans mostly, sometimes an osprey. I had my long lens on a heron when I heard the man with the cast net say 'there,' and I swung around just as two dolphins rolled under the seawall, gold light on their backs.

I got eleven frames. The best one has a dolphin halfway out of the water and, in the corner, two young people leaning on the rail, one of them holding the other's arm. I walked over and showed them on the camera screen. They asked for a copy. I think they will want it someday.
characters: the couple in the corner of my best frame

parts: I eat dinner on the same bench at the marina end of the park on Saturdays. Around dusk someone started playing a harmonica, one slow tune I almost recognized, over and over. It came from the boats, or the path behind me, or the water, depending on the wind.

I walked the whole seawall looking for whoever it was. Nobody had a harmonica. Nobody else seemed to hear it. It stopped when the streetlights came on. I have hummed it all week trying to name it. If you were playing, I would love to know the song.
characters: the harmonica player I never found
